messages.content: What is the acceleration a ball will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with a velocity of 5 m/s?

function.name: calculate_maximum_height
function.description: Calculate the maximum height an object will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with an initial velocity, ignoring air resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity in meters per second. This is a float type value.

gravity.description: The acceleration due to gravity in meters per second squared, default value is 9.8. This is a float type value.

message.content:
When you throw a ball straight up, its motion is governed only by gravity once it leaves your hand (ignoring air resistance).  
Gravity provides a **constant** acceleration directed toward Earth’s center:

\[
a \approx 9.8~\text{m s}^{-2}\quad (\text{downward})
\]

So irrespective of whether the ball starts at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), or any other launch speed, the acceleration acting on it while it travels through the air stays roughly \(9.8~\text{m s}^{-2}\) downward.  

(If you’re interested in how long it takes to stop rising and start falling, we can compute that too.)
message.reasoning:
The user asks "What is the acceleration a ball will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with a velocity of 5 m/s?" They likely want gravitational acceleration downward (i.e., -9.81). But they might misunderstand; maybe they think about acceleration at top? Actually when thrown upward, it decelerates until zero velocity at peak then accelerates downwards under gravity. So acceleration remains constant g (~9.8 m/s^2 downward) regardless of speed.

Thus answer: acceleration magnitude ~9.8 m/s² downward. Provide explanation. No need to call tool because no calculation needed.
